title: Control Testing
summary: Control testing is the evidence-based evaluation of whether a stated control is designed to meet its objective and whether it actually operated throughout the period under review. Design effectiveness asks whether the control, as written and implemented, would prevent or detect the risk if performed as described. Operating effectiveness asks whether it did so in practice, and is tested by inspection of records, inquiry of the performer, observation of the task, and re-performance of the control by the tester. Because controls run repeatedly, testers define the population of occasions on which the control should have operated, then select a sample spread across the whole period rather than a convenient recent window. Results are recorded as exceptions, which are assessed individually and in aggregate to decide whether the control is deficient and how severe that deficiency is. The common mistake is accepting a management assertion or one screenshot as proof, or testing an automated control once and assuming it ran unchanged for a year.

beginner.definition: A control is any rule or tool that lowers a risk, such as asking for two approvals before a payment. Control testing means checking whether that control really works. It is not enough to say the rule exists on paper. You look for proof that people followed it over a period of time. Then you write down what you found.
beginner.whyItMatters: A control that nobody follows gives a false sense of safety. An auditor or a customer may ask you to prove that your controls worked all year. If you cannot show evidence, you may fail an audit or lose a contract. Testing also finds controls that worked once and then quietly stopped. It turns a claim on a slide into something you can defend with facts.
howItWorks: Describe the control clearly, including who performs it, how often, and what proof it leaves behind.
Decide the period you will test, and build a complete list of the times the control should have run.
Choose a sample from that list, or test everything when the number of events is small.
Gather evidence by inspecting records, watching the task, asking questions, or repeating the check yourself.
Record each exception, then judge whether it was a single slip or a sign the control is not working.
Agree a repair with an owner and a date, and test again later to confirm the problem is closed.
beginner.example: Imagine an office where the fire alarm is meant to be tested every Monday. A manager signs a sheet saying the system is fine. A proper check means picking several Mondays at random and asking for the test record for each one. You also watch a test happen and press the alarm button yourself. If two Mondays have no record, the alarm may have been broken for weeks. Control testing follows the same patient method.
takeaways: Test whether the control operated, not only whether it is written down somewhere.
Pick evidence from across the whole period, because one good day proves very little.
Record exceptions honestly and follow each one until an owner fixes it.

objectives: Explain what a control is and what control testing is meant to prove.
Distinguish design effectiveness from operating effectiveness.
Describe common testing methods such as inspection, observation, inquiry and re performance.
Explain how sampling and populations are used when testing across a period.
Describe how exceptions and deficiencies are recorded and remediated.
